questions.problem:
Consider the following geometric sequence:

$$
243,\,-162,\,108,\,-72,\,…
$$

The common ratio of this geometric sequence is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence is the constant we multiply by to get to the next term. In other words, it is the ratio of consecutive terms.

Therefore, the common ratio for our sequence is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{(-162)}{243}=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$

questions.problem: Given that $50$, $5x$, and $12.5x$ are the first three terms of a geometric sequence, find $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The first three terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=50,\,{a}_{2}=5x,\,{a}_{3}=12.5x.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{5x}{50}=\frac{x}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{12.5x}{5x}=2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}2.5 & =\frac{x}{10} \\ 25 & =x \\ x & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $8$, $6x$, and $10x$ are the first three terms of a geometric sequence, find $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The first three terms are

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=8,\,{a}_{2}=6x,\,{a}_{3}=10x.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{6x}{8}=\frac{3x}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{10x}{6x}=\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x}{4} & =\frac{5}{3} \\ 3x & =\frac{20}{3} \\ x & =\frac{20}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $-1,\,-6,\,-36,\,…$

II. $1,\,-4,\,-16,\,…$

III. $2,\,7,\,12,\,…$
questions.worked_solution:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-6)}{(-1)}=6 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-36)}{(-6)}=6\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{(-4)}{1}=-4 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-16)}{(-4)}=4\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is also not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{7}{2} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{12}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequence I could be a geometric sequence.

Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $120,\,80,\,30,\,…$

II. $-243,\,27,\,-3,\,…$

III. $225,\,45,\,9,\,…$
questions.worked_solution:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{80}{120}=\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{30}{80}=\frac{3}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{27}{(-243)}=-\frac{1}{9} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-3)}{27}=-\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is also geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{45}{225}=\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}} & =\frac{9}{45}=\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequences II and III could be geometric sequences.

Find the common ratio of the following geometric sequence.

$$
90, \: -30, \: 10, \: -\dfrac{10}{3}, \: \ldots
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence is the constant we multiply by to get to the next term. In other words, it is the ratio of consecutive terms.

Therefore, the common ratio for our sequence is

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{(-30)}{90} = -\dfrac{1}{3}.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving for a Variable Using the Common Ratio
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $x$, $3x$, $36$ are the first three terms of a geometric sequence, find $x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The first three terms are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=x,\,{a}_{2}=3x,\,{a}_{3}=36.\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio of the first two terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{3x}{x}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{36}{3x}=\frac{12}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by equating the values for $r$ and solving for $x,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =\frac{12}{x} \\ 3x & =12 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying Geometric Sequences
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $2, \: 4, \: 8, \: 16, \: \ldots$

II. $1, \: -\dfrac{1}{3}, \: \dfrac{1}{9}, \: -\dfrac{1}{27}, \: \ldots$

III. $4, \: 8, \: 12, \: 16, \: \ldots$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{4}{2} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{8}{4} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{3}}=\frac{16}{8} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is also geometric. Again, for each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{(-\frac{1}{3})}{1} & =-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{(\frac{1}{9})}{(-\frac{1}{3})} & =-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{3}}=\frac{(-\frac{1}{27})}{(\frac{1}{9})} & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence III is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{8}{4} & =2 \\ \frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{12}{8} & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequences I and II could be geometric sequences.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the following sequence:

$$
1,\quad\:\: 3,\quad\:\: 9,\quad\:\: 27,\quad\:\: 81,\quad\:\: \ldots
$$

Notice that each term is ${\color{blue}3}$ times the previous term:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14204584/assets/9a3af8dd763aa0ab6b176a3a9d711ead4d029e2cebef823f906403be5fc38786.png)

A sequence like the one above, where each term is found by multiplying the previous term by a fixed constant, is called a **geometric sequence**. 

This fixed constant is called the **common ratio**, and is denoted by $r.$ In this particular case, the common ratio is $r={\color{blue}3}.$
